meta.title: Who really said "This is one race of people for whom psychoanalysis is of no use whatsoever"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No evidence Freud ever said it. The line is an unsourced quip about the Irish, popularized as a modern paraphrase in the 2006 film The Departed.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'This is one race of people for whom psychoanalysis is of no use whatsoever'?
meta.ogDescription: No evidence Freud ever said it. An unsourced quip about the Irish, popularized as a modern paraphrase in the film The Departed (2006).

answer.label: Not Sigmund Freud — an unsourced saying popularized by a film
answer.authorDates: Traced in print to Anthony Burgess (1980); broadcast to a mass audience by the 2006 film The Departed
answer.sourceLine: No text, letter, lecture or interview by Freud contains this line, and researchers who have gone looking — including Irish Times columnist Frank McNally — concluded he almost certainly never said it. The wording is a modern paraphrase; screenwriter William Monahan put a version of it in Matt Damon’s mouth in The Departed (2006), and the germ of the idea traces back to Anthony Burgess in 1980, who reported that an unnamed follower of Freud — not Freud himself — divided psychology into “Irish and non-Irish.”

source.excerpt: This is one race of people for whom psychoanalysis is of no use whatsoever.
trail: The version quoted here is the bare wording widely reproduced on quote aggregators such as Goodreads, always credited to Freud but never with a citation.
In The Irish Times, Frank McNally searched for a source and concluded “much as we would love him to have done, he never said any such thing,” tracing the notion to Anthony Burgess in 1980.
IrishCentral discusses the quote via The Departed and gives no Freud citation, concluding its origin may never be known.
Snopes filed it under the flat headline “No Evidence Freud Made This Snark About the Irish.”
source.excerptNote: The line circulates in several forms — often expanded to name the Irish (“The Irish are the one race for which psychoanalysis is of no use whatsoever … because they already live in a dream world”). None of the variants has ever been traced to a Freud text.

source.rightsNote: Because the line cannot be tied to any specific Freud work — and appears to be an anonymous modern paraphrase rather than a passage from a datable, identifiable text — no copyright status can honestly be asserted. The screenplay of The Departed (2006), which popularized one version, is itself in copyright, but the floating quotation predates and differs from it.

author.name: Sigmund Freud
author.heading: The man it’s pinned on
author.bio: Sigmund Freud founded psychoanalysis and reshaped how the twentieth century thought about the mind, dreams and the unconscious. His vast published output — the Standard Edition runs to 24 volumes — is heavily catalogued and searchable, which is precisely why the absence of any Freudian source for this quip is so telling. No serious Freud scholar or collected-works index records him making this remark about the Irish or anyone else.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source located. Earliest documented discussion of the idea: Anthony Burgess (1980), reported in Frank McNally, “The Full Irish, Freud,” The Irish Times, 2014. Popular modern wording: William Monahan, screenplay, The Departed (Warner Bros., 2006).
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘This is one race of people for whom psychoanalysis is of no use whatsoever’?” Last verified 10 Jul 2026.

copyAttribution: Misattributed to Sigmund Freud — no source in his works; a modern quip popularized by the film The Departed (2006).

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on Freud
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet” misattribution: a clever one-liner attached to psychoanalysis’s most famous name, repeated so often it became ‘common knowledge’ — yet no one can point to where Freud wrote or said it.

items.why: No letter, lecture, case study or line in the 24-volume Standard Edition contains this remark. Writers who searched for it, including The Irish Times’ Frank McNally, came up empty and concluded he “never said any such thing.”

The line that put the quip in front of millions is spoken by Matt Damon’s character in Scorsese’s film; it is a modern paraphrase of a saying already circulating, not a quotation from Freud, as IrishCentral notes.

items.who: An unnamed follower of Freud, via Anthony Burgess
items.why: The oldest thread The Irish Times could find is Anthony Burgess in 1980, reporting that an unnamed disciple of Freud — not Freud — split psychology into “Irish and non-Irish.” That, McNally suggests, is where the idea took root.

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: an unsourced modern quip about the Irish, spread by a 2006 film, with no line in Freud’s actual writings to support it — per The Irish Times.

context.heading: Why the quote stuck
lead: The remark flatters a cultural stereotype — the dreamy, story-loving, un-analyzable Irish — and hangs it on the one name guaranteed to lend it authority. That combination is exactly what makes a fabricated quotation durable: it feels right, it is quotable, and the ‘Freud’ tag discourages anyone from checking.

Its modern fame is traceable to a single scene in The Departed, after which the line spread across quote sites, opinion columns and psychotherapy blogs, each borrowing the last one’s authority rather than a primary source.
